blocks.title: Canada's role in the Allied Industrial Base
blocks.alt: Matrix of Canada's roles in the strategic compacts of the Allied Industrial Base: where it is essential, holds a substitutable role, or relies on trusted partners.

inlines.v: Each row is a strategic compact in which Canada holds a role or relies on partners. Dark cells are roles allies cannot easily replace; light cells are roles others could fill; dashed cells mark where Canada relies on trusted partners, orange where allied supply still falls short of what allies need.

Figure 3 shows a materials supplier that relies on partners for battery minerals, magnets and wind materials. None of its roles is essential: across the trusted network, other allies could fill each of them, uranium supply included. In wind, the orange cell marks wind materials refining, where allied supply falls short, so the bargain there has to add capacity, not only redirect trade.

blocks.title: What Canada needs to deploy faster
blocks.alt: Bar chart of Canada's deployment need by technology, marking Accelerate and Watch and the main driver of each.

inlines.v: Deployment need by technology, with the largest of its measures: demand adequacy, the gap to national targets, or system need. Review cases, which rest on a single indicator of low confidence, are shown apart in grey and are not deployment priorities.

High deployment priority does not imply high manufacturing priority. The gas-turbine and LNG-plant calls, a Preserve and a Catch Up, are separate capability choices; the gas build-out itself should buy from whichever trusted supplier is ready. Storage, grid, wind and solar are worth watching, not forcing; a small renewables shortfall argues for a market footing, not local content.

sections.title: Strategic agenda — what should Canada do next?

blocks.text: 1. Secure the rare-earth chain with allied partners

inlines.v: Build trusted separation, metal and magnet capacity with allies such as
Japan, Australia and the United States

through co-investment and offtake, and at home where a foothold can be built. Hold stocks sized to bridge the years until that supply qualifies, screen inbound investment in trusted capacity, and phase in limits on adversary sources in critical uses as it qualifies. No developing partner qualifies in this step; the AIB places new capacity in

blocks.text: 2. Keep cell and pack making competitive and secure its control software

inlines.v: Expand cell and pack production with finance for expansion, workforce and supplier development, tied to benchmarks, with the gate open to allied and conditional investment. Put battery-management and communications software behind the High fence: trusted-source rules for firmware and remote access, certification and monitoring, and limits on over-the-air updates by untrusted vendors.

blocks.text: 3. Build battery materials refining on the nickel chemicals base

inlines.v: Canada's anchor is its export share of refined battery materials, corroborated in nickel chemicals by a supplier role in the AIB. Tie production incentives, first-of-a-kind finance and workforce development to benchmarks, with sunsets, and keep the gate open to licensing and joint ventures that transfer capability in lithium, cathode and anode materials.

blocks.text: 4. Make mineral dependence deliberate and supplier roles reliable

blocks.text: 6. Accelerate gas networks, keep sourcing open and narrow protection

inlines.v: Deploy gas networks faster through infrastructure, permitting and competitive procurement, with trusted-supplier conditions on public deployment support. Keep
